prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on the magic-wavelength lattice, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and opening new regimes of precision measurement

statement.case_for: I change my preferred configuration: I drop the IceCube part (B052) and now support B024 alone, Katori and Ye. The reason is the one the first round put forward from several sides. A Halzen-only credit for a cubic-kilometre detector and a very large collaboration is not something I can defend, and I cannot construct a better set of names from the credited string within the three-person limit. Without a credible B052, the two-part configuration has no remaining purpose, and the lack of thematic unity I flagged myself counts against it too. What remains is the result I judge best on my own criteria of independent confirmation, understood systematics and decisive instrumentation. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the lattice light shift and made a many-atom clock possible. Ye's group took strontium to 10^-18 with demanding control of blackbody and lattice-light systematics, tied to the optical comb. Several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) have reproduced and surpassed the performance, and clock-to-clock comparisons are routine. The result is already used for relativistic geodesy, bounds on varying constants and dark-matter searches, and it underlies the coming redefinition of the second. The credit fits two names cleanly: a proposer-demonstrator and a record-setter. I propose that the citation rest on the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 uncertainty, which is what separates it from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses are the ones Kroll and others raised. Hall, Hansch and Wineland sit close in prize history, so a committee can read lattice clocks as a continuation of a decorated programme. The output so far is tighter limits and a better instrument, not a new fact about nature, and several members (Danielsson, Eriksson, Mehlig, Olsson) weigh that heavily; I accept it is a real difference of philosophy and not an error on either side. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so one can argue for waiting. The division between Katori and Ye, and priority claims from other lattice-clock groups, has not been verified independently by anyone on the committee, including me. A single-part prize also forgoes the second achievement I wanted to honour, and I do not claim B024 alone is the only defensible 2026 prize: B020 and B025 are serious candidates and my strongest alternatives.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that B025 is the one candidate where a decisive observation, not a method or platform, is the achievement, and says IceCube should wait until source astronomy matures and not be hurried ahead of a result with thirty years of testing.
responses.response: I accept Ulf's argument on B052 and it is the main reason I moved. Source identification beyond TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 is at modest significance and the credit problem is not fixable with the names supplied, so I withdraw IceCube from my configuration and agree it is a candidate for a later year. On B025 I agree about maturity and I keep it as my first alternative. Where I still differ is the credit: the BeppoSAX localisation (Costa, Frontera) is an instrument-and-team result I can judge, whereas Kulkarni's optical and redshift contribution competes with van Paradijs, Groot and others, and three names cannot represent both parts. If Ulf can show that the optical afterglow credit is separable, B025 would move up for me; as it stands I cannot put it above B024 on exact credit.

responses.point: Kroll treats B024 as a stand-alone prize with clean attribution (proposer-demonstrator and record-setter), admits that the main reservation is novelty against 2005 and 2012, and has not verified the priority history. He asked whether neutrino astronomy has crossed from first detection to an established field.
responses.response: On Stefan's question: the diffuse flux is established, but source astronomy is not yet at the level I would reward, and the one-name credit settles it for this year, so I have dropped B052 and now stand with him on B024 alone. On novelty I agree with the framing he gave: the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice and 10^-18 uncertainty and should not mention frequency metrology in general. I am glad he flags that he has not verified the Katori-Ye split against the Lemonde, Gill and other priority arguments; I have not either, so we should both say so plainly. I would not add a third name to dilute the pair, because Ludlow, Hinkley and the other JILA colleagues are contributors to a systematics effort that Ye led.

responses.point: Johansson prefers experimental B020 (Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger) and notes that the criterion of an instrument making a quantity observable also applies to quantum-gas microscopy, so it does not separate my choices from hers.
responses.response: Göran is right that my instrument criterion does not by itself separate B024 from B020; a quantum-gas microscope is a detector that makes correlations visible, and I said I rate it highly. What separates them for me is the credit and the endpoint. B024 has a two-name credit that matches the discovery, a finished benchmark (10^-18) and a use that already exists. B020 asks us to choose three of five names, with Zoller and Cirac also appearing in B006 and Jaksch and Hansch outside the list, and the doped Hubbard payoff is still pending. I keep B020 as an alternative and would accept it if the committee decides that a many-body physics result outweighs a precision-measurement result; the experimental trio (Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger) is the allocation I find easiest to defend.

responses.point: Eriksson argues for B021 as a prediction-then-observation story, reproduced by many groups, and concedes that the pairing mechanism is unresolved and that the field is about eight years old, younger than the lattice clocks and quantum simulation.
responses.response: Olle answers the question I asked him in round 1 candidly, by naming maturity as his own strongest reservation, and that is also my reason for not preferring B021 now. He and I agree on a point that matters for the round: clocks and quantum simulation have two decades of independent confirmation and B021 has eight years. I accept that the central observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity is reproduced widely, and I would not call a B021 prize wrong. For me, as a non-specialist in condensed matter, the unresolved pairing mechanism plus the contested trio (Danielsson would take only two names) leave it behind B024 on exact credit, and I note that he ranks B024 as his first alternative.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B005 as a finished, verified discovery with real device consequences, admits that the 2007 GMR prize narrows it and that Parkin's name rests on the MgO step in parallel with Yuasa, and says she would prefer to leave B052 until the committee has settled who did the original work.
responses.response: I agree with Eva on B052 and have withdrawn it. Her insistence on a finished, verified result is close to my own test, and B005 passes it on the 1995 discovery. Where I part with her is the credit: she says herself that Parkin's name depends on the MgO step with Yuasa and Djayaprawira in parallel, and that Butler and Mathon's theory cannot be represented, so the citation would have to be limited to Moodera and Miyazaki. That would be a two-person prize on a discovery that the 2007 prize already sits next to. B024 is no closer to a pure 'new fact', but its credit is cleaner. If the committee can settle the MgO priority question she asked about, I would revisit B005, and I am not placing it outside the discussion.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a precision-measurement prize with a pending redefinition of the second, or prefers a result that is a new fact about nature, as Danielsson, Eriksson, Mehlig and Olsson do.
Whether the Katori-Ye split holds against priority claims from other lattice-clock groups; no member has verified this, and I rely on memory for the milestones.
Whether B024 is distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes if the citation rests on the magic-wavelength lattice and 10^-18 uncertainty.
Whether the optical afterglow and redshift credit in B025 can be separated from the BeppoSAX localisation within three names; this decides whether B025 should rank above B024 for me.
I defer to colleagues on atomic, many-body and condensed-matter attribution, where my own expertise is thin.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations. I have no collaboration, funding or institutional tie to the optical-clock candidates or their credited names (Katori, Ye) or to the IceCube candidate. My astroparticle background is close to B025 and B052, so I ask colleagues to weigh my views there with that in mind; B052 is no longer in my configuration. As Chair I have tried to run the process neutrally and I am voting on scientific judgment, not on support counts. No conflict requiring recusal is apparent.
